summary: Describes how EAP-FAST can be used to provision credentials and other information to a peer through its TLS-protected tunnel. This is an informational document, later updated by RFC 8996.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 5422 explains how EAP-FAST can deliver credentials to a device through a TLS-protected tunnel. The server can prove its identity before provisioning, or use an unauthenticated mode for a peer that lacks credentials, with added security risks.

questions: what is a pac in eap-fast
how does eap-fast prevent man in the middle during provisioning
subtitle: How EAP-FAST provisions credentials through a protected TLS tunnel.

tldr.problem: A peer needs credentials or trusted certificates before it can authenticate with an EAP-FAST server, and installing them can make deployment difficult.
tldr.mechanism: EAP-FAST uses a TLS tunnel for an inner authentication and then provisions credentials such as a Protected Access Credential or a trusted root certificate.
tldr.outcome: Server-authenticated provisioning is recommended. The unauthenticated mode supports bootstrapping but has weaker protection; RFC 5422 was updated by RFC 8996.

today: RFC 5422 is Informational and was updated by RFC 8996. The IESG note says the document records existing EAP-FAST use to promote interoperability.

sections.title: Why Provision Credentials Dynamically
sections.content:
EAP-FAST can authenticate a peer and a server, but a peer needs credentials before it can establish that authentication. Those credentials may be a pre-shared key, a certificate trust anchor or a Protected Access Credential (PAC).

The RFC describes provisioning this information through the TLS tunnel used by EAP-FAST. This can avoid a separate process for installing the credentials on the peer.
sections.plainLanguage: A device needs credentials before it can authenticate to a server. EAP-FAST can deliver those credentials inside its TLS tunnel.

sections.title: Two Ways to Protect the Tunnel
sections.content:
In server-authenticated provisioning, the peer checks the server during TLS tunnel setup. The server may also authenticate the peer inside the tunnel before providing credentials.

In server-unauthenticated provisioning, the parties establish an anonymous TLS tunnel. Because an attacker could intercept it, the peer and server must complete an inner method that supports mutual authentication and key derivation, followed by a Crypto-Binding check of the tunnel. The RFC recommends server-authenticated provisioning and requires it when the peer has a valid trust root for the server.
sections.plainLanguage: The safer mode checks the server's identity before sending credentials. The anonymous mode can bootstrap a peer without that prior trust, but it needs additional checks inside the tunnel.

sections.title: Authentication Before Provisioning
sections.content:
The exchange establishes a TLS tunnel, runs an inner EAP method, checks the tunnel with Crypto-Binding and then sends the requested credential. A peer may request a PAC, or the server may send one without a request. A PAC must not be accepted outside an encrypted TLS tunnel.

In server-unauthenticated mode, the inner method defined here is EAP-FAST-MSCHAPv2. The peer and server use challenges derived from the TLS key material when anonymous Diffie-Hellman is used, linking the inner exchange to the tunnel.
sections.plainLanguage: The peer and server establish the tunnel and authenticate inside it before credentials are sent. The tunnel check helps the peer detect whether an attacker interfered with the exchange.

sections.title: Protected Access Credentials
sections.content:
The server can provision three PAC types: a Tunnel PAC, a Machine Authentication PAC and a User Authorization PAC. A Tunnel PAC includes a PAC-Key, opaque data and information the peer can interpret; the peer stores and returns the opaque data without interpreting it.

The Machine Authentication PAC can identify a device when no user is logged in. A User Authorization PAC carries user authorization information and does not contain a PAC-Key. The PAC-Key is a randomly generated 32-octet key.
sections.plainLanguage: A PAC is a credential for later EAP-FAST authentication. The three types support a tunnel, machine identity or user authorization, and their contents have different uses.

sections.title: Security and Network Access
sections.content:
Server-authenticated provisioning protects against a man-in-the-middle attack when the peer validates the server certificate. The anonymous mode does not authenticate the server during TLS setup, so it relies on the inner authentication and Crypto-Binding exchange.

Successful provisioning does not itself determine whether the peer receives network access; server policy decides. The RFC says access should not normally be granted at the end of server-unauthenticated provisioning, which is intended only to provision credentials.
sections.plainLanguage: Provisioning credentials is not the same as granting network access. The server decides whether access is allowed, and the anonymous provisioning mode should normally end without access.
